In ancient times, two villages stood on opposite banks of a great river. The upstream village, Highwater, controlled the flow through an ancient dam. The downstream village, Lowmeadow, depended on steady waters for their crops.

One summer, drought came. Highwater's elder proposed a covenant: "We will release water to you, trusting you'll share your autumn harvest. But if we open our dam, we risk our own reserves."

Lowmeadow's elder faced a choice. She could promise anything to receive the water, then withhold the harvest when autumn came. Her people would survive twice over.

But she remembered the old ways. "Send the water," she said. "You will receive half of all we grow."

Highwater released the flow, their own wells running dangerously low. Autumn arrived with abundant crops in Lowmeadow. Some counselors whispered, "Keep it all. They cannot take back the water already given."

The elder refused. She sent sixty percent—more than promised. "They risked everything on our word."

When winter struck both villages, Highwater shared their stored grain freely, remembering Lowmeadow's honor.

The river still flows between them, but now it carries more than water—it carries the memory of trust reciprocated, the foundation of all lasting bonds.
